problem: The chapter's own etymology test says common origin points to polysemy, yet the worked example justifies homonymy by saying the financial and river senses of bank have unrelated histories. That etymological claim is not safe: both senses are commonly traced back to the same Germanic root for a bench/ridge, so a student who applies the chapter's etymology test to bank gets the opposite answer from the one the worked example gives.
fix: Drop the history claim for bank. Say the two senses are felt by speakers to be unconnected and fail the zeugma test, so dictionaries list them as homonyms, and add that etymology is only a rough guide because some homonyms do share a root (for example sole, the fish, and sole of the foot).

problem: The sentence 'She has a good head and a good head for numbers' pairs two uses of head that carry the same sense (intelligence, aptitude), so it tests nothing and does not show the sense relation. Students will also wonder why it is linked to the earlier head of a person / head of a department example.
fix: Use two clearly different senses of head in the zeugma sentence, for example 'She has a good head for numbers and a hat on her head', and state that this coordination sounds much less odd than the bank sentence, so the body-part and ability senses are polysemous.
